title: 9.8 A 50W 98%-Efficiency High-Power Wireless-Charging System with an Acoustic Noise-Reduced Ask Modulation Technique and Internal Hybrid Voltage-/Current-Mode ASK Demodulation
problem: High-power wireless charging (Qi MPP >25W) requires frequent and accurate transmitter-receiver (TRX) communication for safety and signal quality, but ASK modulation can introduce acoustic noise in receiver coil; traditional demodulation approaches are inefficient.
method: 50W Qi wireless power transfer system with acoustic noise-reduced ASK modulation in transmitter and hybrid voltage-/current-mode ASK demodulation in receiver; achieves 98% efficiency with improved communication reliability.

title: 36.7 A 1.54pJ/b 64Gb/s 16-QAM Intradyne Coherent Optical Receiver in 28nm CMOS
problem: Short-reach optical links require higher data rates than noncoherent formats (OOK, PAM-4) can achieve; coherent detection with 16-QAM modulation doubles throughput but demands high-linearity analog signal processing and carrier phase recovery while maintaining low power consumption.
method: A 28nm CMOS 16-QAM intradyne coherent optical receiver implements analog carrier phase recovery (CPR) using a novel phase detector (PD) design. The receiver achieves high-linearity signal processing for 16-QAM without requiring high-complexity digital DSP, enabling efficient short-reach deployment.

title: Architecting Value Prediction around In-Order Execution
problem: In-order processors suffer from stalls when long-latency instructions block younger independent instructions from issuing, and the compiler cannot always find sufficient independent work to fill the pipeline. Conventional branch prediction techniques fail to resolve hard-to-predict (delinquent) branches quickly enough to prevent pipeline bubbles.
method: The paper integrates both address-based value prediction and direct value prediction into an in-order pipeline (based on a scaled-up CVA6 RISC-V core), exploiting the property that in-order execution allows aggressive value speculation without recovery penalties (a mispredicted value simply overwrites its slot when the real result arrives). A reworked cache hierarchy adds a fast first-level cache that can be written speculatively. A 32-entry scoreboard 4-issue in-order pipeline is augmented without full register renaming or out-of-order memory hazard handling.

title: Target-Aware Implementation of Real Expressions
problem: Numerical code running on low-precision accelerators and vector ISAs must simultaneously maximize accuracy and performance, but traditional compiler backends optimize for specific targets without accuracy reasoning, while numerical compilers trade accuracy vs. performance without considering the target hardware environment.
method: Chassis is a target-aware numerical compiler that combines aspects of both traditional compiler backends and numerical compilers. It takes numerical expressions as input, explores accuracy-performance trade-offs, and selects implementations that are optimal for a specific target (accelerator, vector ISA, or library functions), emitting code that matches target-environment constraints. The key mechanism is joint optimization over the accuracy-performance space conditioned on what the target hardware/instruction set can actually execute.

title: PipeLLM: Fast and Confidential Large Language Model Services with Speculative Pipelined Encryption
problem: Confidential GPU computing (e.g., NVIDIA H100 TEE) protects outsourced LLM inference through data encryption, but the encryption module imposes up to 52.8% throughput reduction for OPT-30B and 88.2% for OPT-66B due to synchronous encryption latency on the critical path.
method: PipeLLM overlaps GPU computation with encryption through pipelining, analogously to CPU instruction pipelining. The key challenge is that the encryption module does not know which data to encrypt until the GPU requests it, so PipeLLM introduces speculative pipelined encryption: it predicts the next data requiring encryption by analyzing LLM serving patterns (token generation sequences, KV-cache access patterns), pre-emptively encrypting predicted data ahead of GPU demand. A low-cost pipeline relinquishing mechanism handles mispredictions by falling back without correctness violation.

title: Grasp: Group-based Prediction of Activation Sparsity for Fast LLM Inference
problem: ReLU-fied LLMs (ReLU-based activations enabling sparsity) can skip computation in MLPs with predicted zero activations, but existing sparsity prediction methods suffer from reduced prediction accuracy when dealing with distribution outliers, limiting skipping efficiency and speedup.
method: Grasp is a magnitude-based, training-free sparsity prediction technique building on sign-bit methods for ReLU-fied LLMs. It groups vector elements considering their value distribution within the vector and explicitly handles statistical outliers, allowing more accurate per-element impact estimation. The method efficiently identifies zero activations to enable memory access and computation skipping.

title: FleetIO: Managing Multi-Tenant Cloud Storage with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
problem: Cloud virtualized flash storage (SSD) systems must simultaneously support software-isolated and hardware-isolated tenant instances, but face a fundamental tension between performance isolation (preventing noisy neighbors) and resource utilization efficiency — strong isolation wastes storage, while weak isolation causes long-tail latency.
method: FleetIO applies multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to dynamically manage storage resources across multiple tenants. Each tenant is managed by a separate RL agent that learns policies for I/O scheduling, resource allocation, and admission control. The agents coordinate through shared environment observations to balance per-tenant performance isolation with global storage utilization. The MARL framework enables adaptive responses to changing workload patterns without requiring hand-tuned policies, jointly optimizing tail latency and utilization.

title: 9.11 A 98.3%-Peak-Efficiency Single-Mode Hybrid Buck-Boost Converter with 7mV Maximum Output Ripple for Li-Ion Battery Management
problem: Conventional hybrid buck-boost converters with multiple modes suffer from voltage glitches and output overshoot during transitions; single-mode cascaded designs trade efficiency for mode-transition robustness, suffering from reduced efficiency and large output ripple due to discontinuous current delivery.
method: Single-mode topology cascading a boost and buck bridge using a flying capacitor to reduce switch voltage stress and enable continuous current delivery across operating range, eliminating mode-transition issues and output ripple.

title: Has Machine Learning for Systems Reached an Inflection Point?
problem: It is unclear whether ML-for-systems research has reached a tipping point analogous to AlexNet in 2012, where ML transitions from one of many competing approaches to the dominant methodology. The paper investigates whether systems research has arrived at or is approaching that inflection point.
method: The paper is a position/vision paper that surveys the trajectory of ML-for-systems research across sub-domains (scheduling, compilers, storage, networking, etc.), comparing their adoption curves to known ML inflection points in other fields. It evaluates evidence of maturation indicators such as production deployments, benchmark standardization, and displacement of handcrafted heuristics.

title: Grad: Intelligent Microservice Scaling by Harnessing Resource Fungibility
problem: Microservice applications deployed alongside co-located services suffer resource contention that degrades end-to-end latency; existing auto-scaling solutions focus only on scaling critical (bottleneck) microservices and ignore non-critical microservices, missing resource efficiency opportunities through inter-service resource fungibility.
method: Grad uses three components: (1) a modular learning approach that profiles individual microservice latency as a function of environmental conditions (resource allocation, interference); (2) gradient-based extraction from these profiles to design a scalable optimization module that dynamically selects the optimal set of microservices to scale (both critical and non-critical); (3) an end-to-end latency predictor serving as a real-time simulator to provide rapid feedback during SLA violation response. Evaluated on real microservice benchmarks and production traces.

title: Interleaved Bitstream Execution for Multi-Pattern Regex Matching on GPUs
problem: Bitparallel regex engines compile regular expressions into bitstream programs that expose fine-grained instruction-level parallelism well-suited for GPU execution, but the naive sequential (per-instruction loop-over-data) execution model suffers from poor data reuse — each data block is loaded multiple times across instructions — and high memory consumption from intermediate bitstream state, limiting GPU throughput.
method: The paper introduces an interleaved bitstream execution model in which all bitstream instructions for all patterns are fused into a single loop body executed block-wise, so each data block is loaded once and processed by all instructions before moving to the next. Three key techniques make this practical on GPUs: (1) Dependency-Aware Thread-Data Mapping that resolves cross-block data dependencies — introduced because instructions in later iterations depend on state from prior blocks — via selective recomputation of dependency chains rather than communication; (2) Shift Rebalancing that restructures dependency chains to reduce the depth of synchronization barriers needed between warp threads; and (3) Zero Block Skipping that exploits bitstream sparsity (many blocks evaluate to all-zero intermediate state) to skip computation on zero blocks, reducing total work.

title: Assassyn: A Unified Abstraction for Architectural Simulation and Implementation
problem: Architecture developers maintain two separate codebases—a simulation model for design-space exploration and an RTL implementation—creating coordination overhead, alignment errors, and duplicated effort that slow hardware development. Programming directly in RTL is error-prone and low-productivity, forcing teams to decouple modeling from implementation.
method: Assassyn provides a high-level, general-purpose programming framework built on asynchronous event handling—a behavioral model common to both hardware design and software engineering. Developers write a single Assassyn program; the framework compiles it to both a cycle-accurate simulator and synthesizable RTL, enforcing structural alignment by construction. The asynchronous event abstraction covers a broad class of architectures from pipeline components to out-of-order CPUs and application-specific accelerators.

title: AMuLeT: Automated Design-Time Testing of Secure Speculation Countermeasures
problem: Multiple hardware-based Spectre countermeasures have been proposed and then shown to be insecure, yet there is no automated tool to test speculation security guarantees early in the design phase—leaving designers without rapid feedback during hardware prototyping.
method: AMuLeT is an automated design-time testing framework for secure speculation countermeasures. It generates targeted micro-architectural test programs (a.k.a. litmus tests) that systematically exercise speculative execution paths across possible speculation windows and covert-channel observability conditions. The tool evaluates candidate countermeasures against these tests using a hardware RTL or ISA-level simulator, reporting which Spectre attack variants the countermeasure fails to block. AMuLeT integrates with rapid prototyping workflows to provide early-stage security feedback.

title: APSQ: Additive Partial Sum Quantization with Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design
problem: Input/weight stationary DNN accelerators suffer from excessive memory bandwidth and power consumption due to high-precision partial sum (PSUM) storage and retrieval, accounting for ~69% of power in typical dataflows.
method: APSQ integrates PSUM accumulation into the quantization framework, compressing partial sums to INT8 through grouping and reconfigurable hardware support. The method performs nearly lossless compression on BERT, Segformer, and EfficientViT models by seamlessly combining PSUM quantization with algorithm-level optimizations.

title: 19.7 A 27GHz Fractional-N Sub-Sampling PLL Achieving 57.9fsrms Jitter, -249.7dB FoM, and 1.98µS Locking Time Using Polarity-Reversible SSPD
problem: Mm-wave fractional-N PLLs with sub-100fs jitter face challenges in DTC range reduction at high frequencies where prescalers enlarge DTC range, and suffer from prolonged locking times in sub-sampling PLLs due to small SSPD capture range.
method: The fractional-N sub-sampling PLL (SSPLL) employs a polarity-reversible SSPD (phase detector) that samples both rising and falling edges of the oscillator output, reducing DTC range without requiring prescalers. A low-power TDC-based frequency-locked loop (FLL) enables fast locking in fractional mode by compensating the frequency error beyond ref_clock frequency limits, achieving sub-microsecond locking time.

title: TAXI: Traveling Salesman Problem Accelerator with X-bar-based Ising Macros Powered by SOT-MRAMs and Hierarchical Clustering
problem: Ising solvers with hierarchical clustering for large-scale Traveling Salesman Problems (TSPs) face quality degradation as problem size scales beyond certain extent. Hardware-agnostic approaches underutilize available hardware resources.
method: TAXI uses crossbar (X-bar) based Ising macros solving TSP subproblems via hierarchical clustering without inter-macro data movement, enabling massive parallelism. Spin-Orbit-Torque (SOT) MRAM devices serve as compact, energy-efficient random number generators enabling rapid natural annealing within each macro.
